Mata Hari was a Dutch exotic dancer and courtesan who became a German spy during World War I, though her true allegiances remain murky. She was executed by France in nineteen seventeen, accused of espionage that may have caused thousands of deaths, making her history's most infamous female spy and a symbol of seduction as a tool of statecraft.

Born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in the Netherlands, she reinvented herself as Mata Hari—Eye of the Dawn in Malay—to perform exotic dances in Paris. She became a courtesan and lover to numerous French, British, and German military officers and politicians, gathering intelligence through intimate relationships.

During World War I, she worked as agent H-twenty-one for German intelligence while simultaneously accepting money from France and Britain, playing multiple sides. She was accused of passing French military secrets to Germany, allegedly contributing to French defeats that cost thousands of lives.

In February nineteen seventeen, she was court-martialed and executed by firing squad in Paris on espionage charges. However, historians debate whether she was truly a significant spy or a scapegoat caught in the fog of war. Her trial and execution became a sensational international scandal, cementing her legend as the archetypal spy-courtesan.
